Q.1) What explains the eastward flow of the equatorial counter-current? (2015) (a) The Earth’s rotation on its axis (b) Convergence of the two equatorial currents (c) Difference in salinity of the water (d) Occurrence of the belt of calm near the equator

Ans: B The Equatorial Counter Current is an eastward flowing, wind-driven current which extends to depths of 100-150m in the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.

  • As the earth rotates from west to east, water near the equator tends to move from east to west (due to the prevailing winds). This leads to the formation of Equatorial currents, both North and South of the equator.
  • Now, as the North Equatorial Current and South Equatorial Current take the water from east to the western part of the ocean basins, there is a piling up water in the western parts of ocean basins ( or eastern boundaries of land masses near the equator). This piled up water then flows from west to east, under the effect of gravity, resulting in Counter Equatorial Current (CEC).
PDF p.206
  • So, while the rotation of the earth is the primary causative factor for Equatorial Currents, it is piling up of water and subsequent backflow (convergence of both equatorial currents) under gravity which causes the eastward flow of CEC.
  • More often called the North Equatorial Countercurrent (NECC), this current flows west-to-east at about 3-10°N in the Atlantic, Indian Ocean and Pacific basins, between the North Equatorial Current (NEC) and the South Equatorial Current (SEC).
  • The NECC is not to be confused with the Equatorial Undercurrent (EUC) that flows eastward along the equator at depths around 200m in the western Pacific rising to 100m in the eastern Pacific.

Q.2) Tides occur in oceans and seas due to which among the following? (2015) 1. Gravitational Force of the Sun 2. Gravitational Force of the Moon 3. Centrifugal force of the Earth Select the correct answer using the code given below (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2, and 3

Ans: D Tides are the rise and fall of sea levels caused by the combined effects of the gravitational forces exerted by the Moon and the Sun, and the rotation of the Earth.

  • The periodical rise and fall of the sea level is known as tide. The Moon's gravitational pull is the major cause of a tide. Sun’s gravitational pull and centrifugal force due to the gravitational pull of the earth to a lesser extent so causes types.
  • Tides are very long waves that move across the oceans. They are caused by the gravitational forces exerted on the earth by the moon, and to a lesser extent, the sun. Gravity pulls the ocean towards the moon and high tide occurs.
  • High tides and low tides are caused by the moon. The moon's gravitational pull generates something called the tidal force. The tidal force causes Earth—and its water—to bulge out on the side closest to the moon and the side farthest from the moon.

Q.3) Consider the following statements: 1. In the tropical zone, the western sections of the oceans are warmer than the eastern sections owing to the influence of trade winds. 2. In the temperate Zone, westerlies make the eastern sections of oceans warmer than the western sections Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (2021) (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 and 2

Ans.- C

  • Statement 1 is correct. Warmer water is transported westward in the ocean by the Northeast trade winds in the Northern hemisphere of the tropical zone (as the figure given below shows). So, in tropical zones, the western section of ocean is warmer than eastern sections due to trade winds.
PDF p.207
  • Statement 2 is correct. Similarly, the Westerlies play an important role in carrying the warm, equatorial waters and winds to the western coasts of continents (that is eastern section of the Oceans in temperate zone). Thus, in temperate zones, westerlies make the eastern section of the ocean warmer than the western sections.

CORAL REEFS

  • Corals are marine invertebrates , which exist in colonies composed of numerous individual coral polyps , which are tiny, soft-bodied organisms.
  • Corals secrete calcium carbonate to form hard skeletons , which accumulate over time to create large, underwater structures known as coral reefs.
  • These reefs provide habitat and shelter for a diverse range of marine life and are often referred to as the "rainforests of the sea" due to their high biodiversity.
  • Corals rely on symbiotic algae called zooxanthellae for energy through photosynthesis, and they thrive in warm, clear, shallow waters with abundant sunlight.
  • Necessary conditions:
    • Warm Water Temperatures: Coral reefs thrive in warm tropical and subtropical waters with temperatures typically ranging between 20°C to 29°C . These temperatures support the growth and reproduction of coral polyps.
    • Clear, Sunlit Waters: Corals require clear, sunlit waters to facilitate photosynthesis by their symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) , which provides them with essential nutrients and energy. Adequate sunlight penetration is crucial for the growth and survival of corals.
    • Shallow Depths: Most coral reefs develop in shallow water environments, typically less than 50 meters deep. Shallow depths allow corals to access sunlight for photosynthesis and promote the growth of reef-building corals.
    • Stable Salinity Levels: Corals prefer stable salinity levels within the range of 32 to 40 parts per thousand (ppt). Fluctuations in salinity can stress corals and affect their ability to maintain osmotic balance.
    • Low Nutrient Levels: Coral reefs thrive in oligotrophic (nutrient-poor) waters . Excessive nutrient runoff from land-based sources can lead to eutrophication, which promotes the growth of algae that can outcompete corals for space and resources.
    • Moderate Wave Action: Moderate wave action helps to oxygenate the water and remove sediment , promoting coral growth and reef development. However, excessive wave energy from storms or strong currents can damage coral reefs.
  • Other type of Corals:
    • Hard Corals:
      • Also known as stony corals or reef-building corals.
      • Secrete calcium carbonate skeletons, which contribute to the formation of coral reefs.
      • Examples include branching corals like Acropora and massive corals like Porites.
    • Soft Corals:

IMPACTOFCLIMATECHANGEONCORALREEFS

PDF p.208
      • Lack a hard skeleton and have flexible structures.
      • Often referred to as gorgonians or octocorals.
      • Include sea fans, sea whips, and sea pens.
    • Cold-water Corals:
      • Found in deep, cold waters, including polar regions and temperate seas.
      • Adapted to low light levels and cooler temperatures compared to tropical corals.
      • Examples include species of Lophelia, Paragorgia, and Primnoa.
    • Black Corals:
      • Typically found in deeper waters, ranging from 30 meters to over 300 meters deep.
      • Have a dark appearance due to the presence of a protein called melanin.
      • Often prized for their use in jewelry and ornamental pieces.
      • Found in India in Gulf of Mannar region, along with other corals.
  • Types of Coral Reefs:
    • Fringing Reefs:
      • Found close to the shoreline, directly adjacent to land.
      • Develop along the edges of continental coastlines or islands.
      • Characterized by their shallow depths and proximity to land, with the reef crest often exposed during low tide.
      • They might create small lagoons, known as boat channels .
    • Barrier Reefs:
      • Parallel to the shoreline but separated from land by a lagoon.
      • Form farther offshore

compared to fringing reefs and are separated from the mainland by a deep

lagoon.

      • Barrier reefs can stretch for long distances and are often associated with large oceanic islands or

continental landmasses.

    • Atolls:
      • Circular or horseshoe-shaped reefs surrounding a central lagoon.
      • Formed from the gradual subsidence of volcanic islands or seamounts over time, leaving behind a ring-shaped coral reef.
      • Atolls are often found in the open ocean, far from continental landmasses, and may contain several small islands or islets within the lagoon.
  • Coral Bleaching:
    • Coral bleaching occurs when corals expel the symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) living within their tissues , leading to a loss of color and vital nutrients.
    • Bleached corals appear white or pale due to the loss of pigmented algae.
    • This may be temporary or permanent.
    • Bleaching weakens corals and can lead to their death if the stress is prolonged.
    • Factors Responsible for this:
      • Elevated Water Temperatures : High water temperatures, particularly during periods of ocean warming associated with climate change, can trigger coral bleaching.
      • Ocean Acidification: Increased carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere lead to ocean acidification, which can weaken coral skeletons and make them more susceptible to bleaching.
      • Pollution: Pollution from agricultural runoff, sewage, and coastal development can increase stress on corals and contribute to bleaching events.
PDF p.209
      • UV Radiation: Excessive exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation, often exacerbated by clear skies and calm seas, can also induce coral bleaching.
      • Tectonic Activity: Sudden exposure of the corals above the sea level due to land upliftment. Or drowning of corals to non-photic zones due to subsidence.
      • Overfishing: Fish help keep coral reefs clean. If they are removed, sediments and non-useful algae start accumulating over the corals and suffocate them.
      • Diseases: Pathogenic diseases may also at times force the coral polyps to expel the zooxanthellae.
      • Irresponsible Tourism: This may cause pollution, sedimentation, and in certain cases diseases in the corals.
    • Massive coral bleaching event is ongoing since Jan 2023. IMPACT OF CLIMATE CHANGE ON CORAL REEFS
  • Coral Bleaching: Rising sea temperatures due to global warming are the primary culprit. Bleached corals are weakened and more

susceptible to diseases.

    • Example: The Great

Barrier Reef in Australia has experienced

large-scale bleaching events in recent years, jeopardizing its vast coral ecosystems. Currently, 4th mass bleaching event going on since Feb 2023.

  • Ocean Acidification: Increased absorption of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere by the oceans leads to acidification. This makes it harder for corals to build their calcium carbonate skeletons, hindering their growth and survival.
    • Example: Coral reefs in Florida, USA, have shown signs of reduced growth and weakened skeletons due to ocean acidification.
  • Increased Storm Intensity: Warmer ocean temperatures contribute to stronger storms and hurricanes. These storms can physically damage coral reefs through strong waves and generate large amounts of sediment that can smother corals.
    • Example: Coral reefs in the Caribbean have suffered extensive damage from recent hurricanes, hindering their recovery from other stressors like bleaching.
  • Corals in India:
    • Indian reefs have also experienced several bleaching events in recent decades, with significant damage reported in the Gulf of Mannar and the Andamans.
    • In March 2024, coral bleaching events have been reported from Lakshadweep.
    • These events threaten the vibrant coral ecosystems and the associated biodiversity.
    • Pollution from coastal development, destructive fishing practices, and sedimentation from rivers can exacerbate the impacts of global warming on Indian coral reefs.

OCEANIC DEPOSITS

  • Terrigenous Deposits:
    • Derived from land-based sources , such as rivers, glaciers, and wind-blown dust.
    • Found primarily on continental margins , including continental shelves and slopes.
    • Examples include sand, silt, and clay, as well as larger particles like gravel and boulders.
  • Biogenous Deposits :
    • Composed of remains of marine organisms , such as shells, skeletons, and coral fragments.
    • Accumulate on the seafloor over long periods.
    • Found in both shallow and deep ocean environments , including continental shelves, slopes, and abyssal plains.
    • Biogenous deposits include :
PDF p.210
      • Calcareous Ooze : Composed primarily of calcium carbonate shells and skeletons of foraminifera, coccolithophores, and other calcareous organisms. Found in warmer, shallower waters.
      • Siliceous Ooze : Made up of silica-based remains of diatoms, radiolarians, and sponge spicules. Found in colder, deeper waters.
  • Hydrogenous Deposits:
    • Formed through chemical precipitation from seawater .
    • Found in various oceanic environments , including continental shelves, slopes, and deep-sea hydrothermal vent areas.
    • Examples include:
      • Manganese Nodules : Formed of manganese, iron, and other metals precipitated from seawater onto the seafloor.
      • Phosphorite Deposits : Consist of phosphate minerals precipitated from marine sediments.
  • Cosmogenous Deposits:
    • Derived from extraterrestrial sources , such as meteorites and interplanetary dust.
    • Found distributed throughout the oceans , with higher concentrations in deep-sea environments.
    • Examples include microscopic meteorite particles and cosmic dust grains.

DEAD ZONES

Formation:

Consequences:

Examples:

HowtoCombat?

  • Dead zones, also known as hypoxic zones , are areas in oceans and large lakes where oxygen levels become so low that most marine life cannot survive.
  • Causes: The primary culprit behind dead zones is nutrient pollution , particularly excess nitrogen and phosphorus. This pollution often comes from:
    • Agricultural runoff: Fertilizers used in farming can be washed away by rain, carrying these nutrients into rivers and ultimately into coastal waters.
    • Sewage discharge: Untreated or inadequately treated sewage can also contribute excess nutrients.
    • Industrial waste: Certain industries may release nitrogen and phosphorus into waterways.
    • Wind Deposits: A massive algal bloom off the coast of Madagascar was triggered by dust blown from drought-stricken regions of southern Africa. The dust contained nutrients like iron and phosphorus that acted like fertilizers. Formation:
  • When these nutrients reach coastal waters, they trigger a rapid growth of algae. This phenomenon is called an algal bloom . As the algae die and decompose, they sink to the bottom, where they are consumed by bacteria. This bacterial decomposition process consumes a large amount of oxygen dissolved in the water. Consequences: The spread of dead zones poses a serious threat to marine ecosystems, with cascading effects: Loss of Marine Life: When oxygen levels become depleted, fish, shrimp, and other marine organisms suffocate and die. This disrupts the food chain and can lead to ecosystem collapse. Dead zones can become "ecological graveyards" devoid of most marine life. Economic Damage: Dead zones can have a significant economic impact on fisheries, tourism, and other industries that rely on healthy marine ecosystems. As fish populations decline, fishing communities suffer economic losses, and tourism to affected areas can decrease. Public Health Risks: Decomposition of organic matter in dead zones can release harmful toxins and bacteria. This can contaminate seafood and pose a risk to human health if affected fish are consumed. Examples:
  • Northern Gulf of Mexico: One of the world's largest dead zones occurs annually in the Gulf of Mexico, primarily due to agricultural runoff from the Mississippi River basin.
  • Baltic Sea: This semi-enclosed sea suffers from chronic oxygen depletion due to
PDF p.211

nutrient pollution from surrounding countries.

  • Black Sea: The Black Sea has a naturally occurring dead zone in its deep waters due to limited circulation and high organic matter content. How to Combat?
  • Reducing Nutrient Pollution: Implementing stricter regulations on agricultural practices, improving wastewater treatment, and promoting sustainable farming methods are essential to curb nutrient runoff.
  • Monitoring and Management: Regular monitoring of water quality and implementing measures to manage nutrient loads in vulnerable areas can help prevent dead zone formation.
  • Public Awareness: Raising public awareness about the causes and impacts of dead zones is essential for promoting behavioral changes and supporting policies that address this environmental threat.

OCEAN RESOURCES:

  • Biotic Resources:
    • Edible Resources:
      • Fish: Tuna and salmon are abundant in the Pacific Ocean, while cod fisheries are prominent in the North Atlantic. Sardines are found in the Mediterranean Sea and off the coast of Peru.
      • Shellfish: Shrimp and crabs are harvested in the Gulf of Mexico and along the coast of Alaska. Lobsters are abundant in the waters of Maine and the North Atlantic, while oysters are farmed in the Chesapeake Bay and along the Gulf Coast.
      • Seaweed: Japan is a major producer of seaweed, particularly nori, used in sushi. Other countries like China, Korea, and Indonesia also cultivate seaweed for culinary and industrial purposes.
    • Non-Edible Resources:
      • Marine Pharmaceuticals: Marine organisms from coral reefs in the Caribbean and the Great Barrier Reef in Australia have been studied for their potential pharmaceutical properties.
      • Coral Reefs: The Great Barrier Reef in Australia, the Coral Triangle in Southeast Asia, and the Caribbean Sea are renowned for their rich coral reef ecosystems.
      • Pearls: Pearl farming occurs in regions like the South Pacific, particularly in countries like Japan, China, and Indonesia, where pearl oysters are cultivated for their pearls.
      • Seal and Whale Products: Seal fur and whale blubber have historically been harvested in regions such as the Arctic and Antarctic, though regulations have limited commercial harvesting in recent years.
  • Non-Biotic Resources:
    • Energy Resources:
      • Oil and Gas: Offshore oil and gas reserves are found in regions such as the North Sea, the Gulf of Mexico, and the Persian Gulf.
      • Renewable Energy: Tidal energy, Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion, Wave energy; Offshore wind farms are located in the North Sea, the Baltic Sea, and along the coastlines of countries like the United Kingdom, Germany, and Denmark. Wave energy converters are being tested in regions with strong wave action, such as the Pacific Northwest and the Atlantic coast of the United States.
    • Mineral Resources:
      • Dissolves salts , especially NaCl.
      • Manganese Nodules (Poly-Metallic Nodules): Found on the abyssal plains of the Pacific Ocean, particularly in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone. Recent discovery states that these nodules, also known as Polymetallic nodules, are an important source of “dark oxygen”, sustaining the life in the ocean bottom regions.
      • Phosphorite Deposits: Located off the coast of countries like Morocco, Peru, and the United States, where upwelling currents bring nutrient-rich waters to the surface.
  • Intangible Resources
PDF p.212
    • Regulating Services (Environmental Balance)
      • Climate regulation : Oceans absorb ~90% of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases.
      • Carbon sink : Absorb ~25–30% of anthropogenic CO₂; “blue carbon” ecosystems like mangroves and seagrass sequester it long-term. In fact, recent research has shown that the ocean's surface absorbs significantly more carbon dioxide than previously believed, especially the upper layers.
      • Heat & circulation regulation : Ocean currents redistribute heat, influencing monsoons and global climate.
      • Weather & water cycle regulation : Evaporation drives rainfall, storms, and global hydrological balance.
      • Coastal protection : Coral reefs, mangroves, wetlands reduce storm surges, erosion, and flooding.
    • Cultural & Recreational Services
      • Tourism & recreation : Beaches, diving, surfing, cruises fuel coastal economies.
      • Cultural & spiritual values : Sacred seascapes, heritage of coastal communities.
      • Education & research : Source of marine knowledge, climate science, biodiversity studies.
      • Aesthetic & inspiration : Oceans inspire literature, art, and human imagination.
    • Supporting Services (Underlying Systems)
      • Oxygen production : Phytoplankton generate 50–60% of Earth’s oxygen .
      • Biodiversity hotspots : Coral reefs, estuaries, deep-sea vents harbor immense species diversity.
      • Nutrient cycling : Recycle nitrogen, phosphorus, and carbon essential for global food webs.
      • Habitat provision : Support breeding, nursery, and migratory grounds for marine life.

LAW OF SEA

  • The Law of the Sea refers to a body of international law that governs the use of the world's oceans and seas. It encompasses rules and principles regarding maritime boundaries, navigation, exploitation of marine resources, conservation, and protection of the marine environment.
  • United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS): Adopted in 1982 , UNCLOS is the primary international legal framework governing the rights and responsibilities of states in maritime zones. It establishes rules on maritime boundaries, navigation, marine resources, and the protection of the marine environment.
  • Components:
    • Territorial Sea: A belt of water adjacent to a coastal state's land territory, usually extending up to 12 nautical miles (22.2 kilometres ) from the baseline.
    • Contiguous Zone : A zone adjacent to the territorial sea, extending up to 24 nautical miles (44.4 kilometres) from the baseline, where a coastal state may exercise limited control to prevent and punish violations of its customs, fiscal, immigration, or sanitary laws and regulations within its territory or territorial sea.
PDF p.213
    • Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ): An area extending up to 200 nautical miles (370.4 kilometres) from a coastal state's baseline, within which the state has sovereign rights over the exploration and exploitation of natural resources.
    • High Seas: Areas of the ocean beyond the jurisdiction of any state, where all states enjoy freedoms such as navigation, overflight, fishing, and scientific research.

PYQ

Q.1) The most important fishing grounds of the world are found in the regions where: (2013) (a) Warm and cold atmospheric currents meet (b) Rivers drain out large amounts of fresh water into the sea (c) Warm and cold oceanic currents meet (d) Continental shelf is undulating Ans.- C Reasons that determining Fishing grounds

  • The location of major world fishing grounds is governed by many factors:
    • Abundance of plankton
  • coastal waters are beneficial to fish in more than one way—
  • There is plentiful food supply from the erosion of continents, which provide mineral and organic matter.
  • There is enough sunlight penetration, which is critical to the photosynthesis process required by plants.
  • Areas where warm and cold currents meet tend to have high biological productivity, because plankton growth is encouraged by the mixing of cold currents and warm currents.
  • Some of the world’s most productive fishing grounds are located here, where warm and cold currents converge.
  • Examples of these phenomena are the Newfoundland 'banks' and the Sea of Japan.
    • In areas of coastal upwelling high rates of primary production takes

place. Conventional mixing provides plenty of oxygen to sustain life in coastal zones as well as assuring a favourable dispersion of nutrients.

    • Broken coastline with numerous indentations provides excellent berthing facility.
    • Accessible forest resources, which favour the manufacture of fishing boats, jetties, etc.
    • The character of land: Rugged land, which hinders the development of other activities like agriculture and forces the people to go for fishing.
    • Climatic condition: Temperate climate with a temperature of less than 20°C is the best region for marine life.

Quick revise: memory cards, PYQs and alerts#

My condensed layer for this subject, topic by topic: mnemonic cards, PYQ tables with answers and handout alerts.

1 · Oceans and their relief

Basics: hydrosphere ≈ 71% of Earth's surface · 5 oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, Southern · average ocean depth 3,800 m vs average land height 840 m.

🏠 Ocean floor = a house, from the beach inwards:

Part House picture Facts
Continental shelf front porch gentle 1–2°; to ~200 m (up to 500 m); continental crust + sediment; oil & gas, fisheries; North Sea, Gulf of Mexico; Great Barrier Reef (>2,300 km)
Continental slope steep stairs 3–6° (up to 25°); ~200–3,000 m; submarine canyons (Monterey, Hudson); Blake Plateau
Continental rise landing gentle sediment apron at slope base; Amazon rise
Abyssal (deep-sea) plain living-room floor > 2,000 m (2,000–6,000+); flat, fine sediment; polymetallic nodules – Clarion–Clipperton Zone (Hawaii–Mexico)
Trench cellar > 6,000 m; convergent boundaries; subduction, quakes; Mariana Trench
  • Seamounts: ≥ 1,000 m underwater volcanoes (Davidson). Guyots (table mounts): flat-topped seamounts, wave-eroded then submerged (Emperor Seamounts). Hydrothermal vents: mineral-rich water; black smokers; life may have begun here.
  • Terms (with the handout's examples): Strait – Palk · Isthmus – Kra · Archipelago – Japanese · Lake – Baikal, Wular · Bay – Bengal · Cape – Comorin (Kanyakumari; southernmost tip of the Peninsula), Good Hope · Lagoon – Chilika (brackish) · Gulf – Kutch · Peninsula – Indian.

2 · Temperature, salinity, density

Temperature Salinity Density
Key numbers 26.7 °C equatorial mean; 12.7 °C at 45° N/S; deep ocean 2–4 °C; mixed layer to 200–400 m; thermocline = rapid fall deep ocean ≈ 34.7 ppt; Great Salt Lake 220 · Dead Sea 240 · Lake Van 330 cold > warm; high salinity > low; deep > surface
Pattern warmest at equator; Indian Ocean warmest; N. Hemisphere warmer (more land) highest at ~20–30° (subtropics): high evaporation, little rain; lower at equator & poles temperature matters more than salinity
Factors latitude, currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio warm), atmospheric circulation, continentality, depth, season evaporation/precipitation, river inflow, sea-ice (freezing leaves salt behind), currents (Gulf Stream saline; Labrador cold fresher), winds temperature, salinity, pressure

🧂 Salt rule: "Sun + No Rain = Salty." Subtropics (hot, dry) are saltiest; equator and poles are diluted. Enclosed seas keep getting saltier (rivers add salt, evaporation removes water): 220 – 240 – 330 = Great Salt Lake → Dead Sea → Lake Van. Continentality twist: a sea ringed by land is warmer – land "extremes" the sea just as sea moderates the land.

Ocean acidification: pH 8.2 (pre-industrial) → 8.11 (1985) → 8.04 (2024); ~30% more acidic in 200 yrs. More in the Arctic than tropics (cold water absorbs more CO₂). Causes: CO₂ dissolving, volcanoes, agricultural runoff. Effects: coral bleaching, weaker shells, changes in phytoplankton.

Mains 2017 (15m) skeleton – salinity. Intro: salinity = dissolved salts (avg ~35 ppt, deep 34.7). Body (variation): latitude (subtropical high), evaporation vs rain, rivers, sea ice, currents, inland seas (220/240/330). Effects: controls density → thermohaline circulation, stratification (halocline), nutrient distribution, marine habitats and productivity. Close: freshwater from melting ice is now altering salinity and circulation.

Freshwater PYQs. 2013 (ans C): after ice caps/glaciers, the largest share of freshwater is groundwater. 2021 (ans B): ice caps and glaciers hold more than groundwater (≈69% vs 30%); rivers and lakes ≈ 1% (handout also gives 0.3% for surface water). Only ~3% of Earth's water is fresh.

3 · Ocean currents

🌀 West = Warm & Wild; East = cold & Easygoing. Western boundary currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Brazil, East Australian, Agulhas): warm, narrow, fast, strong. Eastern boundary currents (Canary, Benguela, California, Peru, West Australian): cold, broad, slow, upwelling nutrient-rich water. Gyres: N. Hemisphere clockwise, S. Hemisphere anticlockwise (Coriolis). Indian Ocean gyre is anticlockwise.

  • Surface currents (top ~400 m, only ~10% of ocean water; wind-driven) vs deep (thermohaline) currents (density-driven; down-welling at poles, up-welling in tropics).
  • Equatorial system: trade winds push water east → west (also Earth's eastward spin leaves water behind) → deflected by Coriolis into North and South Equatorial Currents → water piles up in the west → flows back east as the Equatorial Counter Current (3–10° N; between the two). PYQ 2015 (ans B): the counter-current flows east because of the convergence of the two equatorial currents (pile-up + gravity), not Earth's rotation directly. (Don't confuse with the Equatorial Undercurrent, deeper at ~200 m.)
  • Circumpolar: Antarctic Circumpolar Current, West Wind Drift – isolate polar water.
  • Gyre members: N. Atlantic – Gulf Stream, N. Atlantic Current, Canary, N. Equatorial; Sargasso Sea in its middle = the only sea without a coastline. S. Atlantic – Brazil, Benguela, S. Equatorial. N. Pacific – Kuroshio, N. Pacific, California. S. Pacific – East Australian, Peru, S. Equatorial. Indian – Agulhas, West Australian, S. Equatorial.
  • PYQ 2021 (ans C, both right): in the tropics the west of an ocean is warmer (trade winds pile warm water west); in temperate zones the east is warmer (westerlies carry warm water to the east side).
  • Factors: latitude, wind, Coriolis, gravity, temperature, salinity, continental margins.

Ekman current: wind-driven; water moves ~45° to the right (N) / left (S) of the wind; layers form the Ekman spiral; causes coastal upwelling (nutrients, fisheries), heat redistribution, El Niño/La Niña links.

Water masses = big bodies with distinct temperature/salinity/density from a source region → set habitat (warm clear = coral; cold nutrient-rich = kelp; deep = specialised life).

AMOC (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation): warm salty surface water flows north (Gulf Stream) → cools, sinks in the North Atlantic (NADW) → flows south at depth. Weaker than at any point in the past millennium (global warming; melting-ice freshwater disrupts sinking). If it weakens: cooler W. Europe, more extreme events, stronger east-coast US hurricanes, less CO₂ uptake, sea-level rise, fisheries shifts. Climate change on currents: weaker thermal and salinity gradients → thermohaline slowdown, less upwelling nutrients and less oxygen in downwelling zones, shifted winds, ice melting from below, biodiversity decline.

Southern Ocean carbon anomaly: absorbs ~40% of the CO₂ taken up by oceans because glacial-melt freshwater forms a light lid that traps carbon-rich deep water below; a "fleeting reprieve" – if the lid weakens CO₂ could rush out. Marine heatwaves: prolonged unusually warm sea; episodes doubled since 1982; warming rate nearly doubled since 2005 (Copernicus); causes – climate change, high pressure, shifting currents, El Niño, feedback loops.

4 · Tides, waves, tsunamis

🌗 Spring tide = SPrung Straight line (syzygy) – new & full moon, Sun-Moon-Earth aligned, highest highs and lowest lows, ~20% higher, twice a month. Neap = Nearly right-angle (quadrature) – quarter moons, forces oppose, lower highs, higher lows. Spring has nothing to do with the season.

  • Cause (PYQ 2015, ans D): gravity of Moon (main) and Sun plus centrifugal force of Earth → bulges on the near and far sides.
  • Most places: two highs + two lows a day (semi-diurnal); a place sees the same tide every 12 h 26 min (Moon takes 24 h 52 min to return). Diurnal tides: Gulf of Mexico, Gulf of Thailand.
  • Tide height depends on: Sun-Moon-Earth distances, funnel-shaped bays/estuaries (amplify), local winds, pressure (low pressure raises sea level).
  • Use: nutrient circulation, temperature moderation, flushing pollution. Tidal bore: wave moving up a narrow river on a high tide, absent at neaps; India – Hooghly; world's biggest – Qiantang (China).
  • Climate change: higher sea level → larger areas tidal; may amplify ranges; threatens mangrove habitats.

Waves carry energy, not water (particles move in circles); wind provides energy. Tsunami: very long seismic sea waves; causes – earthquakes at subduction zones (size ∝ vertical shift), volcanoes, landslides, meteorite impact, nuclear tests. 500–1,000 km/h in deep water, < 1 m high (invisible), slows and grows near the coast; many waves; warning – sea level change, odd ocean behaviour. Rogue waves: freak giants from constructive interference or currents/topography focusing energy (Agulhas Current). Seiche: standing wave sloshing in lake/bay (wind, pressure, quakes, resonance).

5 · Cryosphere & climate change

  • Cryosphere = Earth's ice: 69% of freshwater; albedo; stores methane/CO₂; feeds rivers; affects circulation; GLOFs in Himalaya, Alps, Andes.
  • Melting effects: thermohaline change, winds/jet streams, freshwater (short-term ↑, long-term ↓), lower albedo, GHG release, heavy elements and pathogens released, isostatic rebound and volcanic activity.
  • Arctic: weaker polar vortex → cold spells in N. America/Europe; more temperate storms; new shipping routes (but thick ice drifting into the Northwest Passage); resource access; hundreds of Greenland lakes burst since 2008; trapped mercury leaking. Antarctica: jet-stream weakening; winter heatwaves (mid-July −25 to −30 °C instead of −50 to −60 °C); effects on wildlife and research.
  • Oceans: acidification; SST rise 0.06 °C/decade (1980s) → 0.27 °C/decade now; circulation and nutrient changes.

6 · Coral reefs

🪸 Corals are fussy beach tourists – "Warm, Clear, Shallow, Salt-stable, Light-snack, Mild-waves": 20–29 °C · clear sunlit water (for zooxanthellae algae) · < 50 m deep · salinity 32–40 ppt · low nutrients (oligotrophic – runoff feeds algae that choke them) · moderate waves. Reef types: Fringing = Friend hugs the shore (boat channels) · Barrier = Bodyguard stands off, lagoon between · Atoll = Wedding ring around a lagoon (sinking volcanic island/seamount).

  • Kinds: hard (stony, reef-builders; Acropora, Porites) · soft (octocorals, sea fans) · cold-water (deep, polar/temperate) · black corals (30–300+ m; found in Gulf of Mannar). Reefs = "rainforests of the sea"; corals secrete calcium carbonate.
  • Bleaching = corals expel zooxanthellae (white/pale; may recover or die). Causes: heat, acidification, pollution, UV, tectonic exposure/drowning, overfishing (fish keep reefs clean), disease, tourism. 4th mass bleaching ongoing since early 2023 (handout says Jan 2023 once and Feb 2023 once).
  • Climate impacts: bleaching, acidification (harder to build skeletons), stronger storms. India: bleaching in Gulf of Mannar and Andamans; Lakshadweep, March 2024.

7 · Deposits, dead zones, resources, law

🔠 Four deposit types – "Land, Life, Liquid, Cosmos": Terrigenous (from land: rivers, glaciers, wind; on margins) · Biogenous (organisms) – calcareous ooze (CaCO₃; warmer, shallower), siliceous ooze (diatoms, radiolarians; colder, deeper) · Hydrogenous (chemical: manganese nodules, phosphorite) · Cosmogenous (meteorite dust).

Dead zones (hypoxic): nutrient pollution (N, P: farm runoff, sewage, industry, even wind-blown dust – Madagascar bloom) → algal bloom → dies → bacteria use up oxygen. Effects: marine life suffocates, fisheries/tourism lose, toxins. Examples: northern Gulf of Mexico (Mississippi runoff), Baltic Sea, Black Sea (natural, poor circulation). Fix: cut nutrient pollution, treat sewage, monitor, awareness.

Resources: Biotic – fish (tuna, salmon – Pacific; cod – N. Atlantic; sardines – Mediterranean, Peru), shellfish, seaweed (Japan nori), marine pharma, pearls. Abiotic – offshore oil and gas (North Sea, Gulf of Mexico, Persian Gulf), tidal/OTEC/wave/offshore wind, dissolved salts (NaCl), manganese nodules (a source of "dark oxygen"), phosphorite (Morocco, Peru, USA). Services: oceans absorb ~90% of excess heat and 25–30% of human CO₂ (blue carbon: mangroves, seagrass); phytoplankton make 50–60% of Earth's oxygen.

⚓ UNCLOS 1982 – "12 – 24 – 200": Territorial sea 12 nm (22.2 km) · Contiguous zone 24 nm (44.4 km; customs, fiscal, immigration, sanitary laws) · EEZ 200 nm (370.4 km; sovereign rights over resources) · High seas beyond (freedom of navigation, overflight, fishing, research). Think: a dozen → a day → a double century.

PYQ 2013 (ans C) – fishing grounds: best where warm and cold currents meet (plankton mixing; e.g. Newfoundland banks, Sea of Japan). Other helpers: coastal upwelling, indented coasts, nearby forests for boats, rugged land that pushes people to fishing, temperate water below 20 °C.
